title: Historical-themed illumination display returns to Osaka Castle this winter
summary: The greatest lights in history and the greatest history in lights. I’ve never been too good at history, mainly because I’m terrible at remembering names and dates. But I find when it’s presented in ways other than fact sheets, I can remember what happened a lot more clearly. If you’re like me, then an upcoming […]
details: The greatest lights in history and the greatest history in lights. I’ve never been too good at history, mainly because I’m terrible at remembering names and dates. But I find when it’s presented in ways other than fact sheets, I can remember what happened a lot more clearly. If you’re like me, then an upcoming event in Osaka might be just what you need to handle the long and complex history of Japan. From 20 November to 14 February, the Nishinomaru Garden of Osaka Castle will be brilliantly lit up. Although an illumination display might just sound like a bunch of lights, they tend to go really all out with them in Japan, and the Osaka Castle Illuminage is no exception. This year’s theme is “ Unification of the Realm, Shogun – A Story in Light ,” and boasts almost as many lights as it has subtitles, fittingly using the castle that noted warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi once resided in as a backdrop. In a nutshell, Toyotomi was one of The Three Unifiers of Japan, having worked his way up from the peasant class to grasp control of the entire country. He ordered the construction of Osaka Castle as a base of operations for about a decade before his death in 1598. This illumination event goes far beyond that, however, with an array of dazzling displays both educational and fantastical. Upon entering the garden, guests will follow a corridor of 66 lanterns to help you feel like you’re right in the light show, rather than looking at it from afar. Then, there’s an array of taiko drums , bearing the paulownia crest of the Toyotomi clan, which is still used by the Japanese government today. The drums are meant to be a symbol of the strength the entire country has when working together as one, while also providing the atmosphere of a traditional festival, where these types of drums are often employed. Deeper inside is a light display in the shape of a large nanban trading ship . It is often pointed out that “nanban” literally means “Southern barbarian” and was used for Portuguese traders who successfully reached Japan. However, it was more of a generalized term inherited from Chinese, and many of the goods, arts, and technology brought in by these traders were highly regarded. That’s not to say the “barbarian” label wasn’t used pejoratively as well. There was plenty of discrimination to go around back then too. Speaking of which, the fashions brought in from foreign traders were often well received and had a gradual influence on Japanese culture. It’s something that can be seen in a line of light-based illustrations showcasing how people dressed from 1615 through the large-scale Westernization of Japan in the early 20th century and to the present day. The journey ends at a plaza-like area with neon light displays featuring an assortment of images from Japanese culture , past and present. It’s the perfect place to take a commemorative photo of your visit. This year will also see two new additions to Osaka Castle Illuminage. First, there’s a butterfly swing that is likely to see a lot of action. When rocking back and forth on this four-meter-tall swing set, the wings of the giant butterfly on top move. There’s also a small enclosure that you can enter. Its walls are made of dozens of pinwheels , so when a breeze comes by, they’ll spin and scatter the lights in unexpected patterns. The Osaka Castle Illuminage will be open every day during the period from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. rain or shine. Just remember that although much of Osaka Castle is free to walk around, the Nishinomaru Garden section charges an admission of 2,000 yen (US$13) for adults and 1,000 yen for kids, but babies get in for free. There’s also a really good cake shop nearby if you need to kill some time before it gets dark. Check it out if you can and learn some history or be doomed to repeat it. Just like that guy, whatsisface from the 17th or 18th century. title: Japanese drivers reminded to look out for drunk people passed out on the road this holiday season
summary: As if driving in Japan isn’t hard enough. As the year gradually draws to a close, it’s the time for many organizations to hold their year-end parties. Although many younger people have been increasingly distancing themselves from overindulging in alcohol, drinking is still a major part of these year-end festivities. As a result, this is […]
details: As if driving in Japan isn’t hard enough. As the year gradually draws to a close, it’s the time for many organizations to hold their year-end parties . Although many younger people have been increasingly distancing themselves from overindulging in alcohol, drinking is still a major part of these year-end festivities. As a result, this is also the prime time of year to find business people passed out on benches, the side of the road, or, more problematically, right in the middle of roads. People passing out on roads, or “rojo nekomi” as it’s known in Japan, is not new but a lot of attention has been given to it in recent years after people started heading back to the bars in a post-COVID world. In 2023, about 32 percent of nighttime traffic fatalities involving pedestrians in Tokyo were people who fell asleep on the street. However, alcohol shouldn’t take all the blame for this either. According to the National Police Agency, only 70 percent of rojo nekomi incidents were connected to alcohol, with rising temperatures and an aging population leading to other health issues like heatstroke causing people to faint on the road. ▼ The Japan Auto Federation released a video examining how easy it is for drivers to spot and respond to a person sleeping on the road at night. It’s in Japanese but fairly easy to get the gist of, regardless of the language. In response, various taxi companies have begun working hand-in-hand with the police forces of 32 prefectures to keep an eye out for unconscious people on the streets. The programs seem to be effective as well, because on 9 November, a pair of Tokyo cab drivers were officially commended for assisting street sleepers in two separate incidents. Seijo Police Station invited 70-year-old Yoshitatsu Miura and 28-year-old Kazuki Yamamoto to honor their efforts in rescuing two people from potential death . During the ceremony, Miura explained that he encountered the body at about 2 a.m. and shone his headlights on the person to make them highly visible to other motorists while he called the emergency number for help. In Yamamoto’s case, he felt disappointed that while he was helping the unconscious person, there were other people walking along the street at the time. Some just chose to look the other way. Online comments were happy everything turned out fine in these instances, while some admitted they might not have the courage to get involved like these drivers had. “Everyone was lucky this had a happy ending. If the drivers had hit those people, their lives would have been ruined too.” “Papers are nice and all, but give them some money for that!” “I saw an elderly man sleeping on the road while drunk. I asked if he was OK, but he just yelled at me, so I just moved him out of the way and left. From now on, I’m going to ignore anyone I see like that.” “I wonder what the cutoff is for getting commendations? Tons of people report stuff to the police, after all.” “It’s a common thing in Tokyo near the end of the year.” “If you get so drunk that you sleep on the road, then alcohol isn’t for you.” “I don’t want to get involved, so I probably wouldn’t touch them, but I think I could call someone…” “People who get drunk and fall asleep on the street should be penalized too.” Punishing those who fall asleep on the streets due to drunkenness is a tricky issue. Unlike in Western countries, being even extremely drunk in public is not illegal as long as the intoxicated person is not harassing, assaulting, or damaging anyone or anything. If someone is passed out due to alcohol, the police will detain them for their own protection rather than to arrest them for a crime. That being said, obstructing traffic by lying down or sitting on the road is a crime , punishable by a maximum fine of 50,000 yen (US$317). The problem here is that it’s pretty hard to prove intent on the part of the sleeping person if they’re unconscious at the time of the offense. In Okinawa, where the warm climate has helped to make rojo nekomi a more pervasive problem, the police have been more aggressive and have begun charging repeat offenders with traffic obstruction charges. ▼ This news report features harrowing dashcam footage of a driver stopping right in front of a person sleeping on the road in Itoman, Okinawa. As far as civil litigation goes, the liability for damages or injuries that occurred is considered 30 percent the sleeper’s if during the day and 50 percent if at night. But regardless of how these incidents play out, no good comes of it for anyone involved, so stay safe either by drinking in moderation and getting a safe ride home or by driving at a reasonable speed at night with the appropriate lights in use. title: Yakuza boss sues expressway owners for discrimination against criminals
summary: You gotta fight for your right to be a party to a contract. Ever since 2011, things have been getting rougher and rougher for members of organized crime groups in Japan. That was when a law was passed prohibiting companies from entering into contracts with any known member. That’s why any time you sign up […]
details: You gotta fight for your right to be a party to a contract. Ever since 2011, things have been getting rougher and rougher for members of organized crime groups in Japan. That was when a law was passed prohibiting companies from entering into contracts with any known member . That’s why any time you sign up for a phone or point card , you have to declare on it whether or not you belong to such a group. And with just about everything shifting from cash-based purchases to cashless subscriptions, members of groups such as the yakuza are in an increasingly tight situation. One example can be found on Japan’s many privately owned expressways that require a toll to drive on. It is expected that all toll boths will end cash toll payments in favor of the ETC card system by 2030. An ETC card is like an auxiliary credit card that hooks up directly to your car and is detected automatically as you enter and leave an expressway , billing you the appropriate amount. You need to sign up for one much like you do with a credit card, which means yakuza cannot. Feeling his freedom of movement was hindered by this, a senior yakuza member filed a lawsuit against the operators of expressways, such as NEXCO East , for discrimination . According to the suit, in July 2023, the plaintiff attempted to apply for a special ETC Personal Card that doesn’t require a credit card to use, because he can’t get one of those either. On the application was a checkbox that should be marked if the applicant is a member of an organized crime group. The plaintiff just crossed that whole section out and filled in the rest of the application properly. He was notified a month later that his application was denied. On 10 November, a ruling was handed down in Fukuoka District Court, wherein Judge Masakatsu Tange dismissed the lawsuit , saying that by not being able to use expressways, the restrictions on his rights and freedoms were very minor. In Japan, these roads are completely optional, and it is possible to take similar routes to anywhere in the country. The only major benefits are a lack of traffic lights that will generally ensure a swifter arrival than regular city streets. So, the judge is right in that regard. The yakuza member’s ability to go places is more inconvenienced than it is obstructed. ▼ Though in his defense, the sheer number of red lights on regular streets in Japan is rather maddening. There’s a strange kind of irony to see the yakuza trying to settle matters in a court of law. He also has a point that these restrictive laws against people like him are technically discriminatory, but the matter boils down to whether society deems it right to discriminate against criminals or not. Most online comments regarding this story seem to agree that it is right. “Just walk then.” “He’s not really a credible plaintiff, after all.” “Maybe he should just stop doing illegal stuff?” “That’s on him.” “They’re free to leave that life behind, aren’t they?” “What is this guy talking about? It’s not like he follows the law.” “They shouldn’t even be allowed to have driver’s licenses.” “Even with that kind of ETC card, he’d need a bank account, so how did he get that? Or a lawyer, for that matter?” This law prohibiting doing business with organized crime groups was enacted in 2011, meaning before that it was possible for members to open bank accounts and do lots of other things. That’s why you might see a yakuza member using an old flip phone, because they’re contractually stuck in that era’s tech . Also, many people get bank accounts at a young age, likely before they enter a life of crime. As for hiring a lawyer, that is a constitutional right that cannot be denied, so crime groups are allowed to enter into contracts with attorneys as an exception. That’s also why they can receive medical care, which is also a business transaction but guaranteed by law. Public utility providers also cannot refuse service to anyone by law, but yakuza members technically aren’t allowed to buy property, so I’m not sure where they’ll hook it up. Still, it’s definitely a pain in the butt being a member of the yakuza these days, and by design. It just goes to show that all the goons in the world can’t save you from a passive-aggressive bureaucracy. title: KFC Japan starts selling soft-serve ice cream at select locations, and they’ve even put it in a biscuit
summary: There are many ways to enjoy this new sweet dessert, including as a dip for fried chicken. KFC is world-famous for its fried chicken, but right now it’s turning heads for something else in Japan, with the release of soft-serve ice cream. While that would be big news on its own, what’s even more impressive […]
details: There are many ways to enjoy this new sweet dessert, including as a dip for fried chicken. KFC is world-famous for its fried chicken, but right now it’s turning heads for something else in Japan, with the release of soft-serve ice cream . While that would be big news on its own, what’s even more impressive is the fact that the chain is also sandwiching the soft serve inside a biscuit , creating a brand new dessert on the menu. Available only at select locations, we sent our ice-cream-loving reporter Mr Sato over to our nearest participating branch in Tokyo’s Akihabara to check it out as soon as we heard about it. ▼ Upon arriving, he saw this sign outside, which made him think “When the heck did this happen!?” It really is an under-the-radar release , with information about it scarcely available online, and after asking staff about it, Mr Sato learned that sales only began in late October . Though Mr Sato thought it was a shame that sales hadn’t begun earlier in summer, he certainly wasn’t complaining, and after mulling over the three soft serve cones available – vanilla , chocolate and a mix of both for 290 yen (US$1.81) each – he decided to opt for the “ Biscuit & Soft-Serve Drink Set ” for 680 yen. After placing his order, Mr Sato began to fret as he realised that the warm biscuit might make the soft serve melt faster than usual, which isn’t ideal for someone with the responsibility of photographing the dessert. Determined to get the best photos possible, he rubbed his hands together and prepared his fingers for some fast snapping, which meant that when it arrived, he was ready to grab a selfie with the new dessert. Wasting no time, he turned the camera back towards the dessert, which looked gloriously sinful, but peering closer, he realised that… ▼ …the ice cream already seemed to be melting from the heat of the biscuit. As an experienced soft-serve eater, Mr Sato knows that a variety of factors affect the melting rate of ice cream, including the milk fat content and the amount of air incorporated into it. With this variety looking both milky and airy, he had little time to waste, so he dipped his spoon in for a taste. The flavour was very simple and not particularly strong, giving him neither an especially good nor bad impression. Personally, he thought that Family Mart’s soft-serve actually had more flavour, and was an arguably better deal at just 298 yen, even for the Giga Size. ▼ Still, the creaminess was great, and the ice cream isn’t designed to be eaten on its own, so he tried it with the biscuit. The combination of warm, crispy biscuit and soft-serve ice cream was a winning one. The contrast between crunchiness and meltiness was irresistible, and though you can eat them together as a sort of ice cream sandwich, he found that dipping the biscuit into the soft-serve proved to be another great way to enjoy it. Using the soft serve as a dip turned out to be such a good idea that he decided to try it with some of the other items on the menu. ▼ French fry and soft serve = heaven. After trying the chip dip, it was time to move onto bigger fry, quite literally, with a fried chicken dip. You’d be forgiven for thinking Mr Sato may have gone too far with this idea, but he genuinely recommends giving this combination a try. The sweetness of the cream brings out the savoury saltiness and spices of the chicken, making it taste even better. This unusual but delicious combo reminded Mr Sato of chicken and waffles – popular in the American South, the home of fried chicken – which combines fried chicken with maple syrup. ▼ That thought reminded him that the dessert came with honey maple syrup, so he wasted no time in pouring it over. ▼ The soft serve was now disappearing fast, so after snapping a couple of shots… ▼…he dipped his spoon in for a taste. Though he’d now finished his chicken, so was unable to try it with the honey maple syrup-enhanced ice cream, the drizzle of sweet sauce elevated everything into pure dessert territory. The slightly sweet biscuit, sweet soft-serve and added sweetness from the honey maple syrup created the ultimate triple-sweet treat. Mr Sato dialled up the bliss levels by enjoying it all with a hot coffee on the side, which helped to create the ultimate dessert experience. Trying the soft serve multiple ways is the key to ultimate enjoyment, and Mr Sato highly recommends trying it if you can. As of now, Mr Sato was able to confirm that the soft-serve is currently available at the Akihabara and Asakusa branches in Tokyo, as well as the Minami-machida Grandberry Park branch. There doesn’t appear to be any official information about the rollout, so he recommends checking social media and confirming availability with each branch before visiting. title: Japan making AI app to learn Japanese by talking to anime characters
summary: Japan is developing a new language-learning app that will let anime fans practice their Japanese by having AI-powered conversations with characters from their favorite shows.
details: Trending Modern Warfare 4 Twitch EA FC 27 Wardogs GTA 6 Entertainment Japan making AI app to learn Japanese by talking to anime characters by Nathan Warby Published: Nov 10, 2026, 14:33 Save for later Save for later Crunchyroll Add as a preferred source on Google Follow on Google News Japan is developing a new language-learning app that will let anime fans practice their Japanese by having AI-powered conversations with characters from their favorite shows. Anime and manga have become hugely popular around the world, introducing millions of people to Japanese culture and encouraging many to learn the language themselves. Now, the Japanese government is hoping to capitalize on that popularity with an app that makes learning Japanese feel more like interacting with your favorite characters. Article continues after ad Japan wants anime characters to teach you Japanese As reported by The Japan Times , Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has asked the Japan Foundation to develop an AI-powered language-learning app aimed primarily at younger audiences overseas. Rather than simply studying vocabulary or completing exercises, users would be able to practice speaking Japanese by having conversations with characters from popular anime and manga. While no specific characters or franchises have been announced just yet, it would likely mean users could converse with the likes of Goku from Dragon Ball Z or Monkey D. Luffy from One Piece . Article continues after ad Article continues after ad Crunchyroll The Japan Foundation has previously developed language-learning tools featuring original characters, but licensing restrictions have prevented it from using recognizable faces from existing franchises. For the new app, it plans to negotiate with copyright holders to secure permission to use famous characters. The government hopes the app will encourage more people to learn Japanese while also making lessons accessible in countries where qualified teachers and dedicated language schools are harder to find. It could also give anime fans a new way to engage with the characters they love, although they’ll have to wait to find out which ones will be available. title: Tokyo neighborhood adds new “smart trash cans” to deal with increasing amounts of tourist litter
summary: A high-tech part of Tokyo gets some high-tech help in addressing an overtourism problem and responding to a common traveler complaint. Downtown Tokyo’s Akihabara neighborhood is already one of the most popular tourism destinations for travelers in Japan, by nature of being the country’s center of anime and video game fan culture, and a couple […]
details: A high-tech part of Tokyo gets some high-tech help in addressing an overtourism problem and responding to a common traveler complaint . Downtown Tokyo’s Akihabara neighborhood is already one of the most popular tourism destinations for travelers in Japan, by nature of being the country’s center of anime and video game fan culture, and a couple of new additions to the district are sure to be instant crowd pleasers too. We’re not talking about a new multi-level arcade or manga merch specialty store, though, but a bunch of new public trash cans . Japan’s relative lack of trash receptacles in public spaces has long been among the top complaint from foreign visitors to the country , and it’s an issue that exists even in the most densely developed parts of Tokyo. In recent years, there’s been a noticeable increase in the amount of litter to be seen in the city’s most heavily touristed areas, including Akihabara. ▼ A pile of trash on the sidewalk in Akihabara in January of this year Using funds from the municipal government’s Tokyo Green Up Action subsidy program, Chiyoda Ward, which Akihabara is part of, has acquired 22 SmaGO “smart trash cans” from Tokyo-based tech company Forcetec . Fittingly for Akihabara’s image as a high-tech part of town, these receptacles are actually public trash compactors , using solar power to condense their contents down to one-fifth of their original size. They can also utilize a cloud network to inform maintenance workers of how full the bins currently are, allowing for more efficient coordination of trash pickups. ▼ As is usually the case in Japan, different types of trash go in different containers, so make sure to sort your stuff before you toss it in. The SmaGO trash cans went into service at 10 locations in Akihabara, clustered around Akihabara Station (秋葉原駅 in the map below) and along Chuo-dori (中央通り) , the major shopping street in the neighborhood. The move follows new ordinances requiring more publicly accessible trash cans, and stricter penalties for not using them, which recently went into effect across town in the Shibuya neighborhood . Both districts’ responses to increasing amounts of litter do make one feel a little sad that the current crop of visitors evidently isn’t as concerned with Japan’s customary etiquette norm of carrying your trash home with you if there’s no public place to dispose of it, but hopefully the new initiatives will result in a return to cleaner streets. title: Why people in Japan hardly ever say “sayonara,” and what they say instead
summary: Everyone knows that sayonara means goodbye in Japanese, but goodbye in Japan doesn’t always mean you need to say it. You don’t have to be an anime otaku, foodie with a penchant for matcha and wagyu, or obsessive linguistics enthusiast that know that sayonara means “goodbye” in Japanese. Like loco in Spanish and merci in French, […]
details: Everyone knows that sayonara means goodbye in Japanese, but goodbye in Japan doesn’t always mean you need to say it . You don’t have to be an anime otaku, foodie with a penchant for matcha and wagyu, or obsessive linguistics enthusiast that know that sayonara means “goodbye” in Japanese . Like loco in Spanish and merci in French, sayonara is one of those words that’s so well known internationally that it’s widely understood even by people without any personal connection to its home-country culture. And yet, living in Japan, you’ll very rarely hear anyone actually say sayonara (unless you happen to be in a pre-college school, where students of such ages say it to their teachers at the end of the school day). As a matter of fact, when someone did say it to us the other day, it was startling, even if it was also very appropriate to the specific circumstances that was taking place. But wait, if sayonara isn’t a commonly used phrase, how do people in Japan end conversations? Does one person just wander off once they think the topic has run its course, and the value that Japanese culture places on tacit understanding means that you’re just supposed to infer that the other person said goodbye to you inside their heart? ▼ Wait, Linguistics Samurai! I still had something I needed to tell you! Nope. Japanese actually has several other phrases that take sayonara’s place in the vast majority of daily situations . Let’s take a look at a few, and then circle back to why sayonara usually isn’t used. One of the most common ways to say goodbye when speaking to friends or peers in social situations is ja , which means “if” or “then.” That might seem like a pretty random choice of vocabulary, but there is a logical reason for it, which is that it’s a shortened version of sore ja , meaning “if it’s like that,” or, rendered more naturally in English “in that case” or “well then.” In this situation, sore ja is itself a pared-down version of phrases such as sore ja, kore de kaerimasu (“well then, I’m heading home”), sore ja, ikanakya ” (“well then, I’ve got to get going”), and the like. But if you don’t want to get into the nitty-gritty of why you’re saying goodbye, Japanese social norms allow you to opt out of the explanation and just say “ ja .” Used completely by itself, though, ja can sound a little curt, so to make it a little cordial the all-purpose emphasizer ne , or na among male speakers, is often tacked onto the end. Speaking of adding things after ja, another option for that is mata , the Japanese word for “again.” In this case, it’s included as an abbreviation of things such as mata aimashou (“let’s get together again [sometime]”) or mata ashita (“[see you] again tomorrow”). And to multiply our options even further, if you want to sound a little more polished and polite, you can replace ja with dewa , a more formal word with the same meaning. Mixing and matching these elements will give you all sorts of common ways of saying “goodbye” in Japanese that you’ll hear much, much more frequently than sayonara, such as: ● ja / ja ne / ja na ● dewa ● sore ja / sore dewa ● mata / mata ne / mata na ● sore ja, mata / sore ja, mata ne / sore ja, mata na ● dewa, mata ne / dewa, mata na There are two other Japanese phrases which also don’t translate literally as “goodbye” but regularly get used where we’d say that in English. One of them is otsukarasama desu , which, as we’ve discussed before , more or less means “you must be tired,” but which is commonly said between coworkers when going home at the end of the day, since you’ve both put in a full day of work. Similarly, if you’re going home while someone else is still working, the custom is to tell them osaki ni shitsurei shimasu , meaning “excuse me for going home before you,” which can be shortened down to just osaki ni if you’re on friendly terms with one another. But even knowing all that, sayonara does still mean “goodbye,” so why isn’t it said very often? Because sayonara has a very weighty nuance to it, so much so that it’s mainly used for situations where it’s not just goodbye, but possibly goodbye forever , or at the very least where there’s a very real possibility that you’ll never meet again. ▼ Hearing “sayonara” at the end of a first date is a strong sign that there’s not going to be a second. Because of that, sayonara isn’t something classmates say to each other after grabbing ramen together. It’s what they might say to each other at graduation if they’re all going off to different colleges and there’s no real guarantee they’re going to meet up again. You wouldn’t say sayonara to your coworker Tanaka-san when you clock out on a Friday evening, but you might say it to him at his going away party before his permanent transfer to an overseas office. ▼ If your coworker walks out of the office while waving and saying “Sayonara!”, there’s a good chance she just quit. In other words, when someone does tell you sayonara, it tends to stick with you, because it’s a sign of parting that might be permanent. When someone said it to us the other day, it was a bittersweet moment, so who did we hear it from? The workers at Cold Stone in the city of Kamakura, the very last branch of the chain in all of east Japan , which we visited for one last ice cream treat shortly before it closed on October 31. While he was waiting for his order, our reporter Mr. Sato briefly chatted with the staff about the shop shutting down , and when they handed him his ice cream, they told him thank you, and also “sayonara.” This is Cold Stone’s second time to leave east Japan, and it wouldn’t be a shock if the company decides not to ever take a third shot at it, and that situation was reflected in the employees’ choice of words. Now, none of this means that there’s a taboo against saying sayonara, or that it’s an old-fashioned phrase that feels out of place in the modern world. Sayonara does, though, carry a lot of emotional significance, so it’s a special phrase for special circumstance

title: Tokyo cracks down on Airbnb-style rentals with new laws limiting operator days and more
summary: With tourists’ and residents’ feelings about minpaku racing in opposite directions, wards add new local ordinances onto national laws. “Short-term private vacation lodging” is a bit of a mouthful, and while “Airbnb-style rentals” is more concise, it singles out just one company in what’s become a rapidly expanding sector of traveler accommodations. So today, let’s […]
details: With tourists’ and residents’ feelings about minpaku racing in opposite directions, wards add new local ordinances onto national laws . “Short-term private vacation lodging” is a bit of a mouthful, and while “Airbnb-style rentals” is more concise, it singles out just one company in what’s become a rapidly expanding sector of traveler accommodations. So today, let’s just call them “minpaku,” the term used in Japanese to describe rentals for travelers that weren’t originally zoned or constructed as hotels. Minpaku have been rapidly rising in popularity over the past few years. While the idea of staying in a converted home while on vacation has limited appeal to most Japanese travelers, foreign tourists have shown plenty of enthusiasm for minpaku, especially when coming to Japan in a group of friends or family members who want more communal space for their party than conventional hotels offer. That growing popularity with foreign tourists has simultaneously made minpaku’s presence increasingly unwelcome among local Japanese residents, however, and new ordinances mean that all 23 central wards of Tokyo have now introduced additional rules restricting or limiting their operation, including new bans on accepting guests on weekdays . Houses and apartments are built very close to one another in Japan’s residential neighborhoods. and that creates a sort of etiquette-deterrence situation between long-term residents. The close proximity means that any excess noise or trash generated by one neighbor is likely to affect everyone around them, and vice versa, so residents generally try to stay quiet and clean as a show of mutual consideration, with the baseline tacit agreement of “I won’t cause problems for you, and you won’t cause problems for me.” The importance of maintaining polite long-term relationships within the community doesn’t apply to short-term renters, though, who’ll probably be gone in a few days’ time, and far too often ill-mannered minpaku guests party noisily late into the night, litter in the common-use areas of the buildings they stay in and on the surrounding streets, and otherwise. Minpaku lodgings in Japan started off as a bit of a cottage industry, and the sector managed to build up significant momentum before widespread regulatory measures were put in place. Under the Private Lodging Business Law, minpaku are not allowed to accept guests for more than 180 nights in a calendar year, but many local municipalities have placed additional regulations on top of that. Most recently, Tokyo’s Kita Ward became the city’s 23rd ward to pass its own. As of January 7, Kita Ward will ban the opening of new minpaku in residential areas in which the homeowner is not present when guests are staying in the unit . Requiring the homeowner to be present should, theoretically, increase the minpaku operator’s connection, and personal responsibility, to the surrounding community, creating an accessible contact point for complaints from neighbors or regulatory enforcement by the ward, while discouraging management by remote companies whose facelessness makes it easier for them to ignore grievances. ▼ It’s harder for management to brush off complaints when they have to deal with them in-person. Tokyo’s Taito Ward is also tightening restrictions on minpaku. As of October 1, no new minpaku within the ward will be allowed to accept guests on weekdays, and no new minpaku of any kind will be allowed to open in parts of the ward which are zoned for residential-use only . Taito is also taking action against four minpaku owners who collectively operate eight units within the ward . By law, minpaku operators are required to submit reports on a minpaku’s number of guests and nights in operation every two months, but the owners filed no reports at all for the eight properties for the period between December of 2025 and May of 2026. Taito is now giving the owners approximately three weeks to submit the required documents, and says that failure to do so will result in the owners’ names being publicly announced, followed by forced closures of the minpaku if the non-compliance continues. Other parts of Tokyo are going even farther in their attempts to address residents’ growing irritation at minpaku. Shinjuku Ward, for example, is looking to add legislation that would not only designate areas within it as off-limits for new minpaku, but which would also force currently existing minpaku within them to shut down . In total, Tokyo’s 23 central wards account for roughly 40 percent of all the minpaku in Japan, so it’s likely that other cities will be watching the effectiveness of these countermeasures very closely, and possibly basing their future policies on them in an effort to stave off resident complaints before any such friction with minpaku operators/guests occurs. title: Japanese viewers of Godzilla Minus Zero angered by unusual number of restroom goers
summary: Godzilla films are famous for their subtlety and require complete concentration. Culture Day in Japan was on 3 November, and what better way to celebrate culture than by watching the latest Godzilla film, Godzilla Minus Zero? It was a thought held by many, as the monster movie drew in an amazing 910 million yen (US$5.8M) […]
details: Godzilla films are famous for their subtlety and require complete concentration. Culture Day in Japan was on 3 November, and what better way to celebrate culture than by watching the latest Godzilla film, Godzilla Minus Zero ? It was a thought held by many, as the monster movie drew in an amazing 910 million yen (US$5.8M) on its opening day alone, breaking the record for a live-action film in Japan. However, while the film itself has been incredibly well-received by critics and audiences alike, some moviegoers in Japan complained about their viewing experience . The biggest beef of all was that too many people were getting up to go to the restroom during the film. One post by a social media user said they had an aisle seat during the movie and shortly into it, people had started going to the bathroom one after another, ruining their ability to get into the story. This might just sound like a single oversensitive reaction to this sort of thing, but the post generated significant discussion, with a majority of people agreeing. Others also reported an inordinate number of people going to hit the head during their screenings of Godzilla Minus Zero (or Godzilla -0.0 as it’s known in Japan), including head counts they took during the film. It was enough to make me wonder if I was the weird one for paying absolutely no mind to other people going in and out of the theater in the many movies I’ve seen over the years. There were a few comments to the contrary, saying that complaining about such a thing was going overboard. But there were many more people talking about how hard it was for them to fight the urge to pee towards the end of the movie, which, by the way, includes sitting through the entire credits. That is expected behavior among many moviegoers in Japan , not in the hopes of seeing additional scenes, but purely out of respect for the people who made the film. I’d probably stop short of saying this is “Japanese culture” per se, but it definitely appears to be a prevailing sentiment here. To help get a sense of how people feel about this stuff, here’s a wide sampling of reactions to the situation, covering a range of opinions. “When I saw it, no one went to the bathroom, but when the end credits started, a bunch of people got up right away to leave.” “I think once that first person goes, everyone else feels like it’s okay, and the floodgates open.” “I heard someone call the movie Godzilla vs King Ghidorah vs The Urge to Pee, lol.” “A lot of people got up from their seats here too.” “That’s the problem with blockbuster movies. They draw in people who don’t usually go to the movies.” “When I saw it, the same people went in and out like six or seven times during the movie.” “There was a crazy number of people going to the bathroom!” “I was holding it in so long, it came out like a blast of atomic breath when I finally went.” “Everyone had good manners when I saw it in Wakayama.” “I saw two adults and one child get up during the movie, but no one got up during the credits.” “You should just let it slide. Holding it in isn’t good for you.” “That’s why I always watch on IMAX when possible. The screen is so big you can barely see anyone walking in front of it.” “This is why I never go to movies. Some people might have medical issues, you know?” “I get that it can’t be helped, but someone got up behind me, and I felt bad for all the people that person walked in front of.” “Seriously? Calling people out just for using the restroom? I think etiquette is going in a weird direction.” “I saw Street Fighter and had to go early on. I held it in right to the end of the credits, but it was really close.” “Soooooo many people went to the restrooms. And during one of the scenes where a character laughed, some brat in the row behind me started laughing too. Shut the hell up !” “Yeah, there were tons of people. I wonder why that is.” Regardless of people’s feelings about the situation, the one objective observation here is that an inordinate number of people do seem to be going to the restroom during Godzilla Minus Zero specifically . It’s a bit of a lengthy movie, clocking in at 135 minutes, but some mention that the number of people ducking out for a moment well exceeded that of lengthier movies such as the 172-minute-long The Odyssey . There were numerous theories as to why this is. One was that Godzilla , which dates back to the 1950s, tends to attract an older demographic who may lack the firm bladder control that the youth enjoys. The other is that the fact that a major commercial film opening on a public holiday brought in an inordinate number of people who weren’t “true movie buffs,” or perhaps just decided to see it in on a whim without planning their hydration accordingly. By the way, according to many of the comments, a popular way to suppress the urge to urinate before watching a movie is to eat Bontan Ame candies or daifuku , the latter of which are little snacks made of sweet bean paste covered in mochi. There’s no science to back this up, but who am I to deny people their placebos? There’s also a suspicion that a lot of people didn’t even leave to use a toilet. It could have been that some people weren’t prepared for the scenes of destruction depicted in the film, which can often resemble actual natural disasters and hit close to home for more than a few people in Japan. Regardless of the cause, it seems the one thing we can learn from this is that when watching a movie in Japan, the safe bet is to sit perfectly still and quiet until the very last bit of footage hits the silver screen to avoid the silent wrath and judgmental stares of those around you. title: America’s first-ever permanent One Piece store is now open [Photos]
summary: The Straw Hat Pirates have dropped anchor in Los Angeles. Last month we got word that America would be getting its first-ever One Piece specialty store, and that the wait for it to open wouldn’t be very long. And while it was exciting for fans to look at the concept art for the One Piece […]
details: The Straw Hat Pirates have dropped anchor in Los Angeles . Last month we got word that America would be getting its first-ever One Piece specialty store , and that the wait for it to open wouldn’t be very long. And while it was exciting for fans to look at the concept art for the One Piece Mugiwara Store Los Angeles, now that the shop is actually open we can see what the real thing looks like! November 6 was the grand opening date for the store, which is located at the Westfield Century City shopping center in Los Angeles. Representatives from One Piece animation rights holder Toei and Sony were on hand, as was Japanese professional soccer player Maya Yoshida, who has been playing for Major League Soccer’s Los Angeles Galaxy since 2023. The real star power here though, of course, comes from the characters of the series, and there’s a three-meter (9.8-foot) tall statue of Luffy in his Gear 5 guise standing at the center of the shop , plus plenty of wanted posters of the Straw Hat Pirates posted inside, as shown by Yoshida here. Chopper also gets a special “waverider Chopper” design just for the L.A. shop, showing him surfing the waters presumably just off the California coast. Fittingly for fashion-conscious L.A., there are a lot of exclusive apparel items on offer… …but this being a proper otaku-oriented retailer means that the shelves are also amply stocked with things such as figures and collected manga volumes too. Coolest of all, the One Piece Mugiwara Store Los Angeles isn’t a limited-time, pop-up event, but a permanent place for fans to gather, just like the L.A. area’s recently opened Studio Ghibli specialty shop . title: 41.5 percent of surveyed Japanese middle schoolers don’t think more immigration benefits society
summary: This isn’t a cut-and-dry case of Japanese kids simply becoming more socially conservative, though. Internationalism is becoming an increasingly discussed topic in Japan, as the country’s indigenous population contracts and its number of foreign-national residents increases. This shift is happening quickly enough to be noticed not only by adults comparing the current demographics to how […]
details: This isn’t a cut-and-dry case of Japanese kids simply becoming more socially conservative, though . Internationalism is becoming an increasingly discussed topic in Japan, as the country’s indigenous population contracts and its number of foreign-national residents increases. This shift is happening quickly enough to be noticed not only by adults comparing the current demographics to how they were decades ago, but by adolescents too, and a recent study shows that many of them don’t necessarily see Japan’s growing foreign population as a good thing . University of Tokyo sociology professor Norihiro Nihei conducts a periodic survey of all students at 10 middle schools in Tokyo and the surrounding area in order to track changes in their attitudes regarding social issues. The students are presented with a series of statements, then asked whether they agree or disagree with them. One of those statements is “An increase in the number of foreigners living in Japan will bring many benefits to society,” and in the most recent survey, more than 40 percent said they do not agree . An increase in the number of foreigners living in Japan will bring many benefits to society ● Do not agree at all: 9.6 percent of respondents ● Somewhat disagree: 31.9 percent ● Somewhat agree: 39.8 percent ● Strongly agree: 18.6 percent The percentage of students disagreeing with the notion that immigration would be beneficial to Japanese society nearly doubled between the most recent survey, the data for which was collected in 2025, and the previous iteration of the survey, which was carried out in 2023. An increase in the number of foreigners living in Japan will bring many benefits to society (2023 results) ● Do not agree at all: 3.96 percent of respondents ● Somewhat disagree: 18.3 percent ● Somewhat agree: 50.4 percent ● Strongly agree: 27.4 percent That jump from 22.26 percent who didn’t see increasing immigration as a major positive for society in 2023 to 41.5 percent in 2025 is significant. Nihei is quick to say, though, that this doesn’t signal an across-the-board shift towards right-wing attitudes for young people in Japan . As a matter of fact, he asserts that the way the labels “liberal” and “conservative” are used in Japan and the English-speaking world don’t always perfectly align, and so he wants to put a finer point on how the survey is applying the terms. For the purposes of the survey, Nihei examines what he describes as three indicators of liberal orientation: democratic orientation, tolerance, and autonomous orientation , which the study checks for by presenting a statement representing each. Among them, there were no dramatic drops since the previous survey. Total percentage of agree/strongly agree responses for: ● Rules should be decided through everyone’s discussion. (democratic orientation) 2025: 96 percent 2023: 95.1 percent ● I can accept people with different ways of thinking. (tolerance) 2025: 91.6 percent 2023: 92.1 percent ● It is important to stay true to oneself in any situation. (autonomous orientation) 2025: 83 percent 2023: 87.1 percent There were, however, some large increases in agreement to statements that, within the scope of the study, Nihei cites as indicators of conservative or right-wing orientations of authoritarianism, patriotism, and xenophobia . Total percentage of agree/strongly agree responses for: ● I should follow the instructions of teachers and seniors rather than my own thoughts. (authoritarianism) 2025: 61.3 percent 2023: 57.4 percent ● It is important to love one’s country. (patriotism) 2025: 86.8 percent 2023: 76.9 percent Total percentage of disagree/strongly disagree responses for: ● An increase in the number of foreigners living in Japan will bring many benefits to society. (xenophobia-related attitudes) 2025: 41.5 percent 2023: 23.1 percent It might seem like an odd combination to have continuing extremely high-expressed support for accepting other people’s way of thinking and collectively deciding on the rules while at the same time having a jump in uncertainty as to whether or not more foreigners living in Japan is a good thing for society, but there’s one other factor the survey examines, which Nihei calls “rule strictness,” measured by the participant’s reactions to the statement “People who do not follow rules should be severely punished,” which 70.8 percent of respondents agreed with in 2022. In 2025, the percentage rose to 79.3 percent . The idea of strict enforcement of regulations might seem like something from the conservative school of thought, and Nihei does recognize that such strictness could be seen as the opposite of tolerance, which he treats as a liberal value. However, in an example of one of the many ways conservative and social values may not consist of the same baskets of attitudes in one society as they do in another, Nihei says: “This concept sits on a different axis from the liberal/conservative spectrum. Literally standing at the opposite pole of tolerance, it appears non-liberal on the surface. On the other hand, rule compliance has historically served as a prerequisite for managing a fair society by restraining arbitrary uses of power, thus forming an essential element of liberalism. This is also linked to constitutionalism, having played a key role for the left as well in various forms, such as refusing to tolerate ‘slush-fund lawmakers.’” Taken together, the combination of, to borrow the survey’s terminology, continuing high tolerance at the same time that both xenophobia and rule strictness are increasing could be construed as reflecting a change in Japanese young people’s perception as to how willing foreigners are to follow Japan’s laws and social customs . title: Japanese convenience store offering chance to have your shopping be effectively free for one day
summary: Family Mart offering random reimbursements of up to 100,000 yen (US$630). details: Family Mart offering random reimbursements of up to 100,000 yen (US$630) . Japan’s convenience stores have become world-famous, not only for their convenient locations and operating hours, but for their amazingly wide variety of genuinely tasty snacks , drinks, and even full meals . Really, their only drawback is that they don’t always match the low prices you can find for similar items at supermarkets and drug stores. There’s a potential upcoming exception to that at convenience store chain Family Mart, though, where if luck is on your side everything you buy in your shopping run could be effectively free . On November 11, Family Mart customers who pay using the chain’s Fami Pay app can then play an in-app game, and if they win, they’ll be awarded Fami Pay credit equal to the entire cost of their purchases . The minimum purchase amount required to be eligible to pay is a paltry 111 yen (US$0.70), and the maximum possible prize is 100,000 yen. Technically, the 100,000-yen cap means that it’s possible you won’t be reimbursed for your entire purchase, but it’d be really, really hard to run up a bill greater than that in a single convenience store shopping trip. There’s no need to be concerned about the sharpness of your gamer skills either, as the “game” you play consists entirely of pressing the green start button twice, then being informed of whether you’ve won or not. Winners will immediately receive one yen worth of Fami Pay credit to confirm the win, and the rest of the credit will be added to your account in mid-December, with an expiration date of May 31. This delay is likely to prevent people from overspending and getting a bill they can’t afford to pay if they don’t win, since regardless of whether you win or not, you still need to be able to cover the cost of your bill at the time of purchase. Eligibility to play the in-app game starts at midnight on November 11 and runs until 11:59 p.m. the same day, though the in-app game can be played anytime between November 11 and 13. title: Los mejores animes del verano 2025 según los fans en Japón
summary: Silent Witch, Kaoru Hana y Sono Bisque Doll encabezan el ranking de animes más votados de verano 2025.
details: Anime Los mejores animes del verano 2025 según los fans en Japón Una encuesta japonesa determinó qué títulos conquistaron la temporada de verano 2025. Jin 1 de octubre de 2025 56 Comentarios ADS El portal japonés Anime!Anime! realizó una encuesta entre sus lectores para conocer cuál fue el anime más destacado de la temporada de verano 2025 . Con una oferta variada que incluyó secuelas esperadas, estrenos originales y adaptaciones de éxito, la competencia estuvo reñida. A continuación, te mostramos los resultados completos del ranking. 1. Silent Witch: La confesión de la bruja que no podía hablar Con un 10% de apoyo , el primer lugar fue para Silent Witch , adaptación de la novela ligera publicada por Kadokawa. La historia sigue a Monica Everett , creadora de la magia sin encantamientos, quien debe infiltrarse en una prestigiosa academia para proteger al segundo príncipe. Su carácter tímido y los constantes “quiero volver a mi cabaña en las montañas” contrastan con los momentos en los que revela todo su talento y valentía. Los lectores destacaron la evolución de Monica: “al inicio parecía incapaz de enfrentarse al mundo, pero capítulo tras capítulo mostró un crecimiento entrañable”. También fue aplaudida la construcción narrativa: “cada detalle de la trama tiene un propósito y la animación del opening transmite belleza y simbolismo”. Muchos seguidores pidieron una segunda temporada , señalando que incluso recurrieron a leer la obra original y sus spin-offs tras quedar enganchados con la serie. 2. Kaoru Hana wa Rin to Saku La comedia romántica publicada en Magazine Pocket alcanzó el segundo puesto con un 9% de apoyo. La trama narra la relación entre Rintaro Tsugumi , un chico de apariencia intimidante pero de corazón noble, y Kaoruko Wakuri , una estudiante de un colegio femenino de élite. La interacción entre ambos fue descrita como “refrescante y natural”, logrando conectar tanto con jóvenes como con adultos. Los comentarios de los lectores subrayaron que “la sonrisa de Kaoruko derribó las barreras emocionales de Rintaro de forma conmovedora”. Otros mencionaron que la obra destaca por un elenco secundario atractivo, como Usami , cuyo carisma sorprendió a muchos. En general, se percibió como un relato de juventud sincera y honesta , sin artificios, que deja una sensación positiva tras cada episodio. 3. Sono Bisque Doll wa Koi wo Suru Season 2 En el tercer puesto, con un 8% de votos, se ubicó la segunda temporada de Sono Bisque Doll , el romance protagonizado por Gojo Wakana y Marin Kitagawa . Los fans resaltaron que, tras una espera de tres años, la secuela no decepcionó y mantuvo la esencia de la primera entrega. El entusiasmo de Marin por el cosplay volvió a brillar, y el compromiso de Gojo con la confección de trajes fue considerado una muestra de su autenticidad. “El amor por la creación y la complicidad entre los protagonistas se reflejó en cada capítulo”, mencionaron los encuestados. La inclusión de elementos originales en la adaptación también fue recibida con comentarios positivos: “el staff mostró su cariño por la historia y supo transmitirlo en pantalla”. El resto del ranking Además de los tres primeros puestos, otros títulos también lograron reconocimiento en la encuesta: 4º: Ruri no Houseki 5º: Dandadan Season 2 6º: Seishun Buta Yarou wa Santa Claus no Yume wo Minai 7º: Dr. STONE: Science Future (2º cour) 8º: Takopi no Genzai 9º: Hikaru ga Shinda Natsu 9º: Watashi ga Koibito ni Nareru Wake Nai Jan, Murimuri! La variedad del top demuestra que los fans valoraron tanto la fantasía como las historias románticas y de juventud . Desde propuestas ligeras hasta tramas más oscuras, la temporada de verano 2025 ofreció títulos capaces de satisfacer públicos diversos. ¿Qué anime del verano 2025 fue tu favorito y qué serie habrías colocado en el primer lugar del ranking? title: 10 frases de anime que impactaron más de lo que recordabas
summary: Estas frases del anime, desde Dragon Ball Z hasta JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure, siguen siendo recordadas por su fuerza e impacto.
details: Anime 10 frases de anime que impactaron más de lo que recordabas Un repaso a diálogos de series populares que trascendieron y siguen siendo recordados. Jin 1 de octubre de 2025 65 Comentarios ADS El anime ha dejado incontables escenas memorables, pero algunas frases en particular lograron trascender más allá de la pantalla. Ya sea por la fuerza de los personajes, por el contexto en el que fueron dichas o por cómo resonaron en el doblaje latino, estos diálogos siguen siendo recordados como auténticos momentos icónicos. “No es así… ¡He venido a matarte!” – Dragon Ball Z La frase de Gohan en su enfrentamiento contra Majin Buu marcó un punto de no retorno en Dragon Ball Z. A diferencia de su padre, el joven Saiyajin siempre había mostrado un carácter más pacífico, por lo que escucharle lanzar esta amenaza con absoluta seguridad sorprendió a todos. Fue el instante que confirmó el despertar de su faceta más peligrosa: Gohan Definitivo . “¡No volveré a perder nunca más!” – One Piece Tras su derrota frente a Dracule Mihawk , Zoro hizo una promesa que definió su camino: nunca volvería a ser derrotado. El espadachín de los Sombrero de Paja lloró frente a Luffy y reafirmó su compromiso de convertirse en el mejor del mundo. Esta frase, inmortalizada en el doblaje latino, sigue siendo una de las más recordadas de One Piece . “No voy a morir, voy a ver si realmente estoy vivo.” – Cowboy Bebop En el episodio final de Cowboy Bebop , Spike Spiegel dejó una de las frases más filosóficas del anime. Al despedirse de Faye , el cazarrecompensas explicó que su enfrentamiento contra Vicious no era una búsqueda de la muerte, sino una forma de confirmar que todavía tenía razones para vivir. Este diálogo encapsula la melancolía y crudeza de la serie. “Hay un mundo entero allá afuera, más allá de nosotros y de nuestros sueños.” – Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood Edward Elric pronunció esta frase como parte de una de sus mayores revelaciones. Reconoció que su búsqueda personal por recuperar lo perdido no debía anteponerse a los demás. Fue un momento de madurez y crecimiento que marcó la diferencia en Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood , convirtiéndose en una de las citas más recordadas del doblaje latino. “¡Ayudar sin que te lo pidan, eso es ser un verdadero héroe!” – Boku no Hero Academia Durante su enfrentamiento con Stain , Deku corrigió a Ida con esta frase que resume el ideal de un héroe. En un contexto en el que su vida estaba en peligro, sus palabras resaltaron la esencia del sacrificio y la empatía, consolidando el camino de Izuku como un auténtico símbolo de justicia. “He comprendido que las circunstancias de nuestro nacimiento no importan.” – Pokémon: La película En Pokémon: La primera película , Mewtwo reflexionó sobre su propia existencia con esta frase inolvidable. Creado como un arma, entendió que lo que define a alguien no es su origen, sino lo que decide hacer con su vida. El doblaje latino transmitió a la perfección la fuerza de esta conclusión filosófica. “Si no puedes distinguir entre demonios buenos y malos, no mereces ser un Pilar.” – Kimetsu no Yaiba Tanjiro Kamado lanzó estas duras palabras al Pilar del Viento, Sanemi , tras ver cómo atacaba cruelmente a Nezuko. La frase reflejó la empatía inquebrantable del protagonista, pero también su firmeza al enfrentarse a figuras de autoridad en defensa de lo justo. “Tener más sufrimientos no te da la razón.” – Jujutsu Kaisen Durante el enfrentamiento contra Mechamaru , Panda pronunció esta reflexión contundente. Reconoció el dolor de su rival, pero dejó en claro que la desgracia personal no justifica acciones que dañan a los demás. Un recordatorio fuerte de que el sufrimiento no es una excusa para la injusticia. “No pierdas el tiempo intentando ser el bueno.” – Bleach En medio de la batalla contra Coyote Starrk , el Capitán Shunsui Kyoraku pronunció esta frase que refleja la crudeza de la guerra. En el campo de batalla no hay buenos ni malos, solo ideologías enfrentadas. Este diálogo es recordado por su franqueza y la madurez que transmite en Bleach . “¿Acaso crees que yo, Rohan Kishibe, dibujo manga por dinero y fama?!” – JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure Uno de los personajes más excéntricos de JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure dejó clara su postura con una frase que va más allá del propio anime. Rohan Kishibe declaró que no hacía manga por ambición, sino por pasión al arte. En el doblaje latino, esta línea se consolidó como un auténtico manifiesto de vocación artística. Estas frases no solo definieron a los personajes en sus respectivos momentos, sino que también se convirtieron en auténticos lemas para los fans. Son diálogos que han permanecido en la memoria colectiva gracias a su fuerza, y que siguen demostrando el poder narrativo del anime. ¿Cuál de estas frases recuerdas con más fuerza y cuál agregarías a esta lista? details: Anime A Tale of the Secret Saint confirma estreno de anime en abril de 2026 El anime de Felix Film suma voces destacadas y confirma estreno en abril de 2026. Jin 1 de octubre de 2025 13 Comentarios ADS El sitio oficial de la adaptación al anime de las novelas ligeras A Tale of the Secret Saint , escritas por Touya e ilustradas por chibi , confirmó nuevos miembros de elenco y anunció que la serie se estrenará en abril de 2026 . La producción está a cargo del estudio Felix Film . Entre las incorporaciones se encuentran Tasuku Hatanaka como Desmond Ronan, Daiki Hamano como Zachary Townsend y Tomokazu Sugita como Quintin Agata. El reparto previamente revelado incluye a Shion Wakayama como Fia Ruud, Shinnosuke Tokudome como Zavilia, Yuichiro Umehara como Saviz Nav y Nobunaga Shimazaki como Cyril Sutherland. Equipo de producción La dirección está a cargo de Tomoe Makino , con Naoki Murata como asistente de dirección. Deko Akao supervisa los guiones, mientras que Satomi Kurita diseña a los personajes. La música es compuesta por Kenichiro Suehiro y la dirección de sonido recae en Ryosuke Naya . Origen y trayectoria de la obra La historia debutó en enero de 2019 en la plataforma Shosetsuka ni Naro . Posteriormente, Earth Star Entertainment comenzó su publicación impresa en junio de 2019 . El manga, a cargo de Mahito Aobe , inició en noviembre de 2019 en la revista Comic Earth Star . La franquicia alcanzó más de 3.5 millones de copias en circulación . Además, las novelas ocuparon el segundo lugar en las categorías de Tankobon y Novela en la guía Kono Light Novel ga Sugoi! tanto en la edición 2024 como en la edición 2025. ¿Qué expectativas tienes sobre la llegada al anime de A Tale of the Secret Saint ? title: My Hero Academia is opening a cafe that sells All Might margherita pizza
summary: My Hero Academia is launching a limited-time cafe in Japan that serves food and drinks inspired by the anime’s most popular superheroes.
details: Trending Modern Warfare 4 Twitch EA FC 27 Wardogs GTA 6 Entertainment Food My Hero Academia is opening a cafe that sells All Might margherita pizza by James Busby Published: Sep 29, 2026, 09:58 Save for later Save for later Shueisha Add as a preferred source on Google Follow on Google News My Hero Academia is launching a limited-time cafe in Japan that serves food and drinks inspired by the anime’s most popular superheroes, and there’s even an All Might Magahrita pizza up for grabs. Have you ever looked at a cheesy pizza and felt it needed All Might’s signature smiling face plastered over it? No, me neither, but that doesn’t mean MHA enjoyers don’t deserve to munch on the mighty man’s face. Four new pop-up cafes across Japan will allow you to do just that. Article continues after ad Starting October 16, 2026, My Hero Academia fans can grab a taste of the anime by indulging in an All Might margherita pizza, spicy Bakugo curry, Midoriya mint soda, and other themed menu items. All Might pizza and Midoriya soda headline MHA cafe The main attraction of the cafe collab is the ¥2,090 (around $13.28) pizza box, which lets visitors choose from character-inspired pizzas. Main character Deku’s pizza is topped with basil cream and arugula that reflects his costume’s hood and cape. Article continues after ad Meanwhile, Deku’s childhood friend Bakugo combines meatballs and spicy curry, with crisp pastry and mashed potato details modeled on his explosive powers and fiery costume. Article continues after ad Chefs have also cooked up a gorgonzola and pepperoni pizza that represents the two sides of Todoroki’s Half-Cold Half-Hot Quirk. Todoroki’s father gets a bacon and chili tomato pizza, with the cafe stating it’s been inspired by his Hellflame Quirk. Diners looking for a sweet treat can opt for the Uraka option, as her pizza comes topped with chocolate, marshmallows, vanilla ice cream, whipped cream, and a pink sauce. However, the most visually impressive is none other than the All Might margherita, which comes with his signature smiling face proudly printed onto the cheesy topping. Related Chainsaw Man is opening IRL Reze cafe with anime-themed food My Hero Academia cosplayer turns into terrifying Himiko Toga My Hero Academia cosplayer explodes into action as female Bakugo Article continues after ad 1 of 7 The rest of the menu includes donuts inspired by younger versions of Deku, Bakugo, and Todoroki, plus fries for Uraraka and buffalo wings for Takami. You can also wash it down with seven themed hero drinks, ranging from Deku’s mint and muscat soda to Uraraka’s peach soda topped with cotton candy. Article continues after ad Each character drink costs ¥990 (around $6.30) and comes with a coaster featuring the hero it represents. Fans can also pick up merchandise featuring newly drawn art, including badges, acrylic stands, keychains, pouches, stickers, and clear files. Article continues after ad The My Hero Academi cafes open in Tokyo, Nagoya, and Sapporo on October 16, with Osaka following on October 22. Each location will run for a limited time, with reservations available through the official website. So, if you happen to have a trip planned to Japan and are a big MHA fan, then consider grabbing yourself a hero-themed lunch. It’s not just My Hero Academia that is getting a food-themed collab this year, as Chainsaw Man is opening an IRL Reze cafe with anime-themed food on October 1 . title: Forza Horizon 6 players banned over anime paint jobs
summary: Forza Horizon 6 players in Japan have claimed they’ve been banned for having anime-themed paint jobs on their cars, despite having them in other games.
details: Trending Modern Warfare 4 Twitch EA FC 27 Wardogs GTA 6 Gaming Forza Forza Horizon 6 players banned over anime paint jobs by Connor Bennett Published: Sep 24, 2026, 09:57 Save for later Save for later @kracovia_ (X) Add as a preferred source on Google Follow on Google News Forza Horizon 6 players in Japan have claimed they’ve been banned for having anime-themed paint jobs on their cars, despite having them in other games. Customizing your car in Forza has long been something that fans love to dedicate time to. Many take real-life designs from different racing series, movies, and memes, and put them on the wide range of cars in-game. Anime-themed cars – also known as itasha – have also become a fan favorite over the years. With Forza Horizon 6 being set in Japan , these designs have become even more common to see, with fans downloading them by the dozen. Article continues after ad However, fans in Japan have now claimed that their designs have been removed, with users actually banned from uploading new ones as well. Reddit: Cavalier__ Some normal anime designs celebrate VTubers, manga, and other characters. Anime-themed liveries cause bans for Forza Horizon 6 It was pointed out by Automaton , who noted that some fans have claimed there is a “reporting campaign” going on to see them struck down. “They (the developers) show absolutely no respect for the culture they used as the game’s main selling point,” one player said. “It was peaceful, and itasha were a normal thing. Yet in this installment, set in Japan, the homeland of itasha culture, they’ve become something that is punished.” Article continues after ad Article continues after ad Others noted that some liveries – which are more on the suggestive and adult-themed side of the argument – have been rightfully banned, but that the mass banning has affected those who don’t fall foul of that. “Some were genuinely against the rules, but the vast majority were just regular itasha paint jobs,” another posted ; adding “work in progress” liveries had also seen players receiving bans. フォルツァホライゾン6で今起こってる事 痛車ペインターが一斉ハードウェアBAN、一部は本当に規約違反のものもあったが大半は普通の痛車ペイント 通報している連中は恐らく前回と同じ勢力、マクロ等を組んで一斉通報してハードウェアBANまで追い込んでいる模様… — 松永マグロ (@Maguro_Maznaga) September 21, 2026 As Automaton notes, the game’s code of conduct does prohibit liveries that are, among other things, “sexually inappropriate/suggestive, spam/advertising, personal information.” Related Forza Horizon 5 player slapped with 8,000-year ban for livery they made Forza Horizon 5 “incredibly lazy” vehicle design is getting roasted Forza Horizon 5 devs flamed for ban decision on player’s “sexual” design Article continues after ad “Code of conduct written as vague as possible,” one fan complained. “There needs to be proper communication here,” another urged. As it stands, Playground Games has not commented on things, with some players complaining that they’ve not heard from community support when appealing their bans. Forza Horizon 6 is also set to release on PlayStation in the near future. title: Fan-made LEGO Exodia wins contest to become first-ever official Yu-Gi-Oh set
summary: A fan-made LEGO Exodia model has won the company’s Yu-Gi-Oh contest, meaning it will now be transformed into the franchise’s first official LEGO set.
details: Trending Modern Warfare 4 Twitch EA FC 27 Wardogs GTA 6 TV & Movies Lego Fan-made LEGO Exodia wins contest to become first-ever official Yu-Gi-Oh set by Michael Gwilliam Published: Sep 16, 2026, 15:02 Save for later Save for later 4Kids Add as a preferred source on Google Follow on Google News A fan-made LEGO Exodia model has won the company’s Yu-Gi-Oh contest, meaning it will now be transformed into the franchise’s first official LEGO set. LEGO announced the result of its ‘It’s Time to Duel!’ Ideas challenge after allowing fans to vote between five finalists. The winning model, titled The Heart of the Cards: Exodia, was created by LEGO Ideas user Step_on_a_Brick and depicts Yami Yugi summoning Exodia the Forbidden One. Article continues after ad The build shows the legendary monster emerging from enlarged Yu-Gi-Oh cards, creating an effect where Exodia appears to transform from a 2D image into a massive brick-built figure. In Yu-Gi-Oh, a player can immediately win a duel by gathering all five pieces of Exodia in their hand. The LEGO design similarly puts the monster front and center alongside a brick-built version of Yugi. LEGO Exodia defeats four other Yu-Gi-Oh finalists LEGO first announced its Yu-Gi-Oh contest in February 2026 , inviting fans to submit builds inspired by the Duelist Kingdom and Battle City arcs of the original anime. Article continues after ad Article continues after ad Entries were required to contain between 400 and 2,000 pieces. LEGO ultimately narrowed 264 submissions down to five finalists before handing the decision over to a public vote. Step_on_a_Brick Fans largely welcomed Exodia’s victory. “The best choice to be honest, in terms of brand representation it has the monster, the cards, and the main character,” one Reddit user said. Others were disappointed that the winning build was not designed around minifigures, while some questioned how the first Yu-Gi-Oh set could arrive without Seto Kaiba or his Blue-Eyes White Dragon. Related Dragon Ball’s first-ever LEGO set leak reveals $180 Shenron and Goku An official Yu-Gi-Oh! Lego set is in the works at last Yu-Gi-Oh Crocs collab includes an actual card of a crocodile wearing Crocs Article continues after ad LEGO’s designers will now adapt the concept into a finalized retail product, meaning its design could change before release. The company has not yet revealed a price, piece count or launch date. We’re excited to announce that Step_on_a_Brick’s The Heart of the Cards – Exodia submission will be transformed into the official LEGO Ideas x Yu-Gi-Oh! set! For full details on what happens now: https://t.co/XB4BcNT1Zr Congratulations, Step_on_a_Brick! 👏 pic.twitter.com/0uALMhW9J3 — Yu-Gi-Oh! (@yugioh) September 14, 2026 Step_on_a_Brick will be credited in the set’s instruction booklet and receive 1% of its net sales as royalties. The set follows other fan creations selected for official releases through LEGO Ideas, including a brick-built Godzilla model . It also comes as LEGO expands further into anime, with the company already releasing One Piece and Pokemon products, while a Dragon Ball Z reportedly has nine sets lined up. title: Higurashi mahjong remaster turns matches into life-or-death fights against killer anime girls
summary: Higurashi is getting a mahjong game where players must take part in life-and-death battles against the series’ killer anime girls.
details: Trending Modern Warfare 4 Twitch EA FC 27 Wardogs GTA 6 Gaming Higurashi mahjong remaster turns matches into life-or-death fights against killer anime girls by James Busby Published: Sep 15, 2026, 12:43 Save for later Save for later CITY CONNECTION Add as a preferred source on Google Follow on Google News Higurashi is getting a mahjong game where players must take part in life-and-death battles against the series’ killer anime girls, where cheating, unfair tactics, and death await. Higurashi no Naku Koro ni Jong Remaster is a fresh take on a classic Japanese arcade game from 2009 and is built around two-player Japanese Riichi Mahjong. However, in true Higurashi fashion, the tile-based strategy games aren’t exactly your typical chill Sunday afternoon sessions. Instead, players must do whatever it takes to survive against their killer classmate companions to avoid a brutal demise, unlock new artwork, and get the game’s true ending. Article continues after ad Higurashi mahjong is back According to the Steam page , the Higurashi mahjong remaster features three game modes and an original scenario supervised by original creator Ryukishi07. As for said modes, there’s Oyashiro Mode, which pits you against the likes of Mion and Rena in an intense series of high-stakes mahjong battles. Just like the after-school games Keiichi plays in the original visual novel, players can cheat and use unfair methods to get an edge over their foes. You’ll need to use everything you can to avoid a grizzly death, especially when trying to get to the game’s true ending (you know, the less stabby version). Article continues after ad Article continues after ad For those looking for a more chill session without the fear of being brutally murdered, there’s the Club Mode. While you’ll still be able to cheat your way to victory to avoid penalty games, the developers note that sessions here are more ‘heartwarming’ in nature. Not a bad option for those looking to learn the ropes, or just chill with their favorite characters. Then there’s the Club Mode Extra: Paikuzushi Chapter, which is a newly added mode that features unlockable cutscenes after winning matches. That’s not all either, as there’s a Bonus Gallery where you can enjoy the new illustrations alongside character audio dramas. Related Higurashi creator is joining fans on a tour of the real village that inspired the game Rurouni Kenshin: Everything we know about the 2023 reboot Jujutsu Kaisen: Who is Hiromi Higuruma? Yuji’s ally explained Article continues after ad 1 of 4 Fortunately for those who don’t know how to play mahjong (couldn’t be me), you’ll be pleased to know that there’s an auto mode. By selecting this option, the computer will take control of your moves, so you’ll still be able to experience the story and character animations without having to pick up a beginner’s guide to mahjong. Article continues after ad Higurashi no Naku Koro ni Jong Remaster is currently set for a 2027 launch on Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 5, and PC via Steam in Japan. There’s currently no word on an English release, but given that the original Higurashi and Umineko visual novels are available in the West, we’ll hopefully get our hands on the upcoming release too. Article continues after ad In other Higurashi-based news, the game’s creator will be joining fans on a tour of the real mountain village that inspired the game .
